title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence II
statement:
A **subsequence** of a string is whatever remains after deleting any number of its characters (possibly none, possibly all) while keeping the rest in their original order; the empty string and the string itself both qualify.

Given an array of strings `strs`, call a string an **uncommon subsequence** if it is a subsequence of exactly one element of `strs` and of no other element. Two equal elements at different positions count as different elements, so a string inside both of them is not uncommon.

Return the length of the longest uncommon subsequence, or `-1` if no uncommon subsequence exists.
constraints: strs[i] contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every subsequence of every string and counting where each one appears works, but there are up to 2^10 per string. The key observation removes all of that: if some subsequence `sub` of `strs[i]` appears in no other string, then `strs[i]` itself appears in no other string either (any string containing `strs[i]` would also contain `sub`). And `strs[i]` is at least as long as `sub`. So the longest uncommon subsequence, if any exists, is always one of the whole strings. It is enough to enumerate the strings and test each one against all the others.

## Approach

1. Write `isSubsequence(small, big)`: walk `big` with index `k`, advancing `matched` whenever `big[k]` equals the next needed character of `small`; `small` fits if every character got matched.
2. Keep `best = -1`. For each index `i`, skip it if `strs[i]` is no longer than `best`, since it cannot improve the answer.
3. Otherwise compare `strs[i]` with every other index `j`. If it is a subsequence of any `strs[j]` (including an equal copy), it is not `uncommon`.
4. If it survives every comparison, its length becomes `best`.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`strs = ["aba","cdc","eae"]`. For `i = 0`, `"aba"` is not a subsequence of `"cdc"` (no `a`) nor of `"eae"` (no `b`), so `best = 3`. The other strings have length 3, which is not more than `best`, so they are skipped. The answer is `3`. In Example 2, each `"aaa"` is inside the other copy and `"aa"` is inside both, so the answer stays `-1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · L) for n strings of length at most L: each pair is compared once with a linear two-pointer scan.
- Space: O(1) besides the input.

## Pitfalls

- Duplicates matter: a string equal to another element is a subsequence of it, so it is never uncommon. Compare indices (`i !== j`), not string values.
- A shorter string can still be the answer when every longer string is duplicated or contained, as in `["aabbcc","aabbcc","cb"]` (answer 2).
- Keep the argument order of `isSubsequence(strs[i], strs[j])`: it asks whether the candidate fits inside the other string; swapping the arguments tests the opposite question.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `isSubsequence(small, big)` | whether `small` can be read in order inside `big` |
| `matched`, `k` | characters of `small` matched so far, and the position in `big` |
| `best` | length of the longest uncommon string found, or `-1` |
| `i`, `j` | the candidate string and the string it is compared with |
| `uncommon` | whether `strs[i]` has avoided every other string so far |
